The Torah is a one-sentence principle followed by a single proof text (Psalms 119:157). The Rebbe uses 'וְזֶה שֶׁהִתְפָּאֵר' to equate the abstract principle of machloket with David's concrete experience of pursuers and adversaries — these are bechinas of each other. The Rebbe also equates 'דֶּרֶךְ הַשֵּׁם' with 'עֵדוֹתֶיךָ' via the parallelism of the verse. This yields two packages: one evil (machloket and its instruments) and one good (God's path / His testimonies), with a corresponding eitza chain connecting them (machloket causes deviation from God's path).

packages.label: מַחֲלֹקֶת וְרוֹדְפִים
packages.reason: The Torah opens with the principle that machloket (controversy directed against a person) is a force that can sway him from God's path. The Rebbe then invokes David's verse — 'רַבִּים רוֹדְפַי וְצָרָי' (many are my pursuers and adversaries) — as the bechina of this principle. The phrase 'וְזֶה שֶׁהִתְפָּאֵר' (and this is what David boasted) is the Rebbe's standard bechina marker: David's pursuers and adversaries ARE the bechina of machloket. These two concepts share the same essential nature — they are both expressions of the hostile external force that threatens to displace a person from his spiritual standing. Machloket in the abstract and 'rodoفai v'tzarai' in the concrete are two faces of the same reality. Both are evil-polarity: they represent the opposing force directed against the person of integrity.

packages.label: דֶּרֶךְ הַשֵּׁם וְעֵדוּת
packages.label_en: The Path of God and His Testimonies
packages.reason: The Torah presents the positive counterpart to machloket: what one must not be swayed from. The phrase 'דֶּרֶךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ' (the path of God) appears in the teaching's opening principle, and the verse cited — 'מֵעֵדוֹתֶיךָ לֹא נָטִיתִי' (from Your testimonies I did not turn) — is the Rebbe's bechina for the same concept in David's mouth. The teaching closes by restating the principle: 'לֹא נָטָה מִדֶּרֶךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ' — and this is the exact parallel to 'מֵעֵדוֹתֶיךָ לֹא נָטִיתִי'. God's testimonies (עֵדוֹת) ARE the path of God (דֶּרֶךְ הַשֵּׁם) — they are two expressions of the same reality: the spiritual ground on which a person stands and from which controversy seeks to dislodge him. Both concepts share the same essential nature: the divine anchor that preserves a person's level (מַדְרֵגָה) in the face of external hostility.
